explain: S3 is the standard durable data lake storage for raw and processed data, and it integrates natively with Glue, Athena, and SageMaker. The other options are either compute services or unsuitable for large-scale lake storage.
options: Store raw and curated datasets in Amazon S3 as the central data lake
Store raw training datasets in ephemeral EC2 instance store volumes replicated manually
Keep all raw datasets in SageMaker notebook instance local disks
Load raw data directly into Amazon ElastiCache Redis clusters
q: A team needs durable, scalable storage for raw and processed ML datasets. Which service should hold the data lake?

explain: S3 object keys with date-based prefixes give cheap partitioning that Athena, Glue, and SageMaker can all exploit for faster filtered reads. Random UUID keys or single buckets without prefixes prevent partition pruning.
options: Write all incoming records into one single S3 object with a random UUID key name
Organize S3 objects with date-based prefixes such as year/month/day for partitioning
Store each daily batch inside a SageMaker Studio user profile folder only
Keep every raw file on one Amazon EBS volume attached to a single notebook instance with no partitioning
q: Streaming click events land hourly in S3 and are queried by date. Which key layout best supports efficient date-filtered queries?

explain: Columnar formats like Parquet let Athena and SageMaker read only the needed columns, cutting scan cost and speeding up training data loads. Row-based CSV forces full scans of every column.
options: Keep large training tables as single giant CSV files with no compression at all
Convert analytics tables into multi-megabyte uncompressed JSON lines per record
Store large tabular datasets in Parquet format partitioned by date columns
Archive feature tables as serialized Python pickle objects in S3 buckets
q: A 500 GB tabular dataset is scanned daily by Athena and SageMaker jobs. Which storage format minimizes scan cost and time?

explain: S3 Event Notifications trigger processing as soon as each file arrives, giving near-real-time ingestion without polling. Scheduled full-bucket scans or manual downloads add latency and cost.
options: Run a daily cron job that lists the whole bucket and reprocesses every object found
Ask analysts to download new files manually and upload them to SageMaker Studio
Poll the bucket every hour with ListObjects and copy all files to EBS volumes
Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke Lambda or Glue on each new object
q: New sensor files arrive in S3 unpredictably and must trigger feature processing within seconds. What ingestion pattern should you use?

explain: Lake Formation provides centralized fine-grained permissions on Data Catalog tables and columns, including cross-account sharing. IAM bucket policies alone cannot enforce column-level access.
options: Use AWS Lake Formation with Data Catalog grants for table and column-level access
Grant every analyst AmazonS3FullAccess so all data lake buckets stay open
Share the AWS root credentials with each analytics team for direct S3 access
Copy sensitive tables to public S3 buckets secured only by obscure unguessable key names and shared links
q: Multiple teams share one data lake, but PII columns must be restricted per team. How should you enforce fine-grained access?

explain: Lake Formation governs access to tables registered in the Glue Data Catalog; Athena and SageMaker then respect those grants at query time. It does not replace the crawler or rewrite file formats.
options: Lake Formation crawls raw files and automatically converts every CSV into Parquet
Lake Formation centralizes Data Catalog permissions enforced by Athena and SageMaker
Lake Formation trains ML models directly on S3 data without any ETL pipeline or feature engineering stage at all
Lake Formation replaces Kinesis streams by buffering real-time events durably
q: What is the primary role of AWS Lake Formation in an ML data lake?

explain: A Glue crawler infers schema from raw files and registers partitioned tables in the Data Catalog so Athena and SageMaker can query them. Manually copying files or training on raw paths skips cataloging entirely.
options: Write a custom script that downloads each S3 file to a laptop for manual inspection
Launch an EMR cluster to train the model directly on uncatalogued raw S3 paths
Run a Glue crawler over the S3 prefixes to create partitioned Data Catalog tables
Create IAM users for every file so each object carries its own access policy
q: Thousands of CSV files land in S3 daily with evolving columns. How do you make them queryable with a maintained schema?

explain: The Data Catalog stores table metadata and partitions centrally so Athena, EMR, and SageMaker share one schema definition. It stores metadata, not the data files themselves.
options: It physically duplicates every S3 dataset into a faster proprietary store
It streams live events from Kinesis directly into SageMaker endpoints
It retrains Glue crawlers automatically whenever model accuracy drops
It holds shared table metadata and partitions queried by Athena and EMR
q: What does the Glue Data Catalog provide to Athena, EMR, and SageMaker jobs?

explain: Scheduled crawlers detect new partitions and schema changes so queries keep working as data evolves. One-time manual table definitions go stale as soon as the format drifts.
options: Schedule the Glue crawler to run regularly and update new partitions and schema
Define Athena tables once manually and never update them when file formats evolve over time
Rename S3 objects randomly each day to force Athena to rescan everything
Store schema definitions only in analyst notebooks instead of the catalog
q: Source files gain new columns monthly and new date partitions daily. How do you keep catalog tables current?

explain: Athena runs serverless SQL directly against S3 via the Data Catalog, ideal for quick exploration before building pipelines. Spinning up EMR or Redshift clusters adds setup overhead for ad hoc checks.
options: Load a sample into ElastiCache Redis and query it with hand-written Lua scripts
Run Amazon Athena SQL queries directly against the S3 data lake files
Provision a Multi-AZ RDS cluster and bulk-load the whole lake before querying
Deploy a SageMaker endpoint to serve SQL answers from a trained LLM model
q: An engineer must quickly profile a new 200 GB S3 dataset with SQL before building a pipeline. Which service is simplest?

explain: CTAS with Parquet plus partition columns rewrites data into an optimized layout that makes repeated Athena queries and SageMaker reads much cheaper. Re-saving as bigger CSVs preserves the full-scan problem.
options: Export Athena results to uncompressed CSV files inside a single S3 prefix
Duplicate the raw JSON files into additional buckets in multiple AWS Regions
Use CTAS queries to rewrite data as partitioned Parquet for repeated reads
Increase Athena workgroup limits so expensive full scans simply run longer
q: Repeated Athena queries over raw JSON logs are slow and costly. How should you optimize the data layout?

explain: Kinesis Data Streams supports real-time producers and consumers with per-record processing at low latency, fitting fraud scoring. Firehose is load-and-deliver to destinations without per-record app processing.
options: Use S3 Batch Operations to copy transaction files once per day for scoring
Poll an SQS queue hourly and retrain the whole model on each new message
Buffer events with Kinesis Data Firehose directly into S3 without consumers
Ingest card transactions with Kinesis Data Streams for real-time consumers
q: A fraud model must score each card transaction within seconds of the swipe. Which ingestion service fits best?

explain: Firehose buffers, batches, optionally transforms via Lambda, and delivers to S3 or Redshift without managing consumers. Data Streams is needed only when custom real-time stream processing is required.
options: Use Kinesis Data Firehose to buffer and deliver records to S3 destinations
Build custom Kinesis Data Streams consumers with manual checkpointing that write each record individually by hand
Run a self-managed Kafka cluster on EC2 with manual scaling and patching
Send click events through SES email messages collected into S3 buckets
q: Clickstream events must flow continuously into S3 with minimal operational overhead. Which service should you choose?

explain: Shard count with proper partition keys controls throughput and ordering per key; more shards raise parallel capacity. Retention period and Lambda timeouts do not increase ingest throughput.
options: Extend the stream retention period to seven days to raise per-second throughput
Provision enough shards with a good partition key to match the write rate
Attach a longer Lambda timeout so each record consumes more processing time
Enable detailed CloudWatch alarms because monitoring alone adds more shards
q: A Kinesis Data Stream throttles during peak traffic with a single shard. What scaling action fixes the bottleneck?

explain: Firehose invokes a Lambda function to transform each batch before delivery, the standard way to clean or enrich records in flight. Streams consumers or notebook jobs add unnecessary complexity.
options: Download each delivered S3 file and edit records manually in a text editor
Route Firehose output through SNS topics that discard malformed records
Attach a Lambda transform to Firehose to clean records before S3 delivery
Train a SageMaker model that rewrites Firehose batches after they land
q: Records in Firehose need light cleaning and JSON-to-Parquet conversion before landing in S3. How is this done?

explain: Data Wrangler is the visual low-code Studio tool for exploring, cleaning, and exporting data flows, ideal for analysts avoiding Spark code. DataBrew, EMR, and Glue ETL target heavier or code-based pipelines.
options: Write an EMR PySpark application with custom partitioning and cluster tuning
Build an AWS Glue ETL job with bookmarks and custom Scala transformations
Profile datasets with Amazon Athena DDL statements and manual CTAS scripts
Prepare data visually with SageMaker Data Wrangler flows in Studio Classic
q: An analyst must visually explore and clean tabular data with minimal coding. Which SageMaker tool fits best?

explain: Data Wrangler exports the visual flow as a reusable processing script and pipeline step, so engineers can schedule it in production. Screenshots or manual repetition do not scale or version the logic.
options: Export the Data Wrangler flow as a SageMaker Processing job for pipelines
Take screenshots of the Data Wrangler flow and rebuild every transform manually before each training run
Copy the transformed CSV from Studio to S3 by hand for every new batch
Email the flow definition to engineers who retype each step into Spark
q: A prototype cleaning flow built in Data Wrangler must run automatically in production. What should you do?

explain: DataBrew is the serverless visual data-preparation service with 250+ built-in transforms and profiling, aimed at business users. EMR and Glue require coding and cluster or job management.
options: Process the files with a self-managed Hadoop cluster tuned by hand on EC2
Use AWS Glue DataBrew with built-in transforms and visual data profiling
Write raw MapReduce jobs in Java submitted through the EMR console manually
Query the data with ElastiCache Memcached using custom client-side parsing
q: A business user needs serverless visual profiling and 250+ built-in transforms without writing Spark. Which service fits?

explain: DataBrew jobs scale serverlessly and can be scheduled or attached to datasets for recurring preparation. One-off console clicks or laptop scripts do not scale or track lineage.
options: Rerun the recipe manually in the console whenever someone remembers to do it
Run the transforms in an Excel macro on an analyst laptop every Monday
Schedule a DataBrew job with the saved recipe on the versioned dataset
Ask engineers to rewrite the recipe as Kinesis consumers for batch files
q: A DataBrew recipe cleans weekly sales files. How do you run it reliably on every new arrival?

explain: EMR with Spark handles distributed heavy transformations over terabytes that single-machine tools cannot fit in memory. DataBrew, Wrangler, and Athena suit smaller or interactive workloads instead.
options: Load the terabyte join into one pandas DataFrame on a notebook instance
Clean the data interactively with Data Wrangler on a small sampled subset
Run the aggregation with Athena federated queries paginated by hand daily
Process the terabyte-scale joins with EMR Spark across a managed cluster
q: A 3 TB multi-table join with heavy aggregations exceeds single-machine memory. Which prep approach scales best?

explain: Glue ETL provides serverless Spark jobs with bookmarks, catalog integration, and scheduling for recurring pipelines. Athena and crawlers query or catalog data but do not run recurring transforms.
options: Build a scheduled AWS Glue ETL job with bookmarks writing to the data lake
Run one-off Athena SELECT statements and paste result rows into new hand-managed S3 files each time
Schedule Glue crawlers to rewrite the data files during each catalog scan
Copy raw files between buckets with S3 replication instead of transforming
q: Nightly raw logs must be transformed incrementally into curated Parquet. Which serverless ETL option fits best?

explain: Job bookmarks track processed files so reruns handle only new data, giving idempotent incremental loads. Disabling bookmarks or deleting outputs forces costly full reprocessing.
options: Disable job bookmarks and reprocess the entire multi-year raw history from scratch on every run
Enable Glue job bookmarks so reruns process only newly arrived source files
Delete the curated output before each run to force a complete recomputation
Raise the worker count sharply because extra capacity alone skips old files
q: A Glue job reprocesses all history nightly instead of just new files. Which feature makes it incremental?

explain: The online store serves low-latency per-record lookups for inference, while the offline store holds historical data for training. Reversing them would add latency to live predictions.
options: Serve both training and inference from ad hoc Athena queries over raw unoptimized CSV files
Keep live features in ElastiCache and retrain models only on log files
Use the Feature Store online store for inference and offline store for training
Store inference features in S3 Glacier and training rows in DynamoDB tables
q: A recommendation endpoint needs millisecond feature lookups, plus historical features for retraining. How should Feature Store be used?

explain: The offline store persists point-in-time historical feature values in S3 for training and backfills. The online store keeps only the latest values for real-time serving.
options: The offline store caches SageMaker endpoint responses to speed up inference
The offline store holds IAM policies that govern online store read access
The offline store buffers Kinesis events before they reach the data lake
The offline store keeps historical feature values in S3 for model training
q: What is the purpose of the SageMaker Feature Store offline store?

explain: Ingestion into both stores keeps live lookups and training history consistent from one pipeline. Writing to only one store forces fragile dual writes or stale training data.
options: Ingest features into both online and offline stores through one pipeline
Write features only to the online store and dump endpoint logs for training
Skip Feature Store and join raw S3 files at inference time for each request
Maintain two separate manual CSV exports, one for serving and one for ML
q: A fraud team wants consistent features for live scoring and retraining without skew. What ingestion setup avoids drift?

explain: Point-in-time lookups join features as of the event timestamp, preventing future data from leaking into training rows. Using latest values or random joins leaks information from after the label.
options: Join each training row with the latest current feature values available today in the online store
Query the offline store with point-in-time correctness using event timestamps
Sample random historical feature rows and attach them to unrelated labels
Backfill training sets with features computed after the prediction horizon
q: Training rows must reflect only feature values known at each transaction time. Which offline-store query pattern ensures this?

explain: One-hot encoding turns each category into binary columns without implying false ordering, unlike integer labels. Hashing or target means add collision or leakage risks for simple nominal data.
options: Replace each product category with random integers that imply a false ranking
Encode categories as the mean fraud rate computed over the full dataset
Apply one-hot encoding so each category becomes its own binary column
Hash every category into a single float column with frequent collisions
q: A model consumes a nominal product-category column with 12 values. Which encoding avoids implying false order?

explain: High-cardinality IDs explode one-hot width, so embeddings, hashing, or target encoding with care are preferred. Plain one-hot on millions of IDs creates unmanageable sparse matrices.
options: One-hot encode every user ID because sparse matrices always train faster
Drop the identifier silently even though past behavior strongly predicts churn
Convert user IDs to floats by parsing the string prefix as a decimal number
Use embeddings or hashed features instead of one-hot for high-cardinality IDs
q: A user-ID column has two million distinct values. Why is plain one-hot encoding a poor choice here?

explain: Fitting the imputer on training data only and applying it to validation avoids leaking validation statistics into training. Computing means over all data or dropping everything leaks or wastes data.
options: Fit the median imputer on training data, then apply it to validation folds
Compute imputation means over train plus test data combined before splitting
Delete every row with any missing value even when half of the collected dataset vanishes entirely
Fill missing test values with the test labels to improve imputation quality
q: A numeric column has 8% missing values. Which imputation workflow avoids data leakage?

explain: Missingness itself can be predictive, so adding a binary indicator preserves that signal alongside imputation. Deleting rows or filling with labels either wastes data or leaks the target.
options: Delete all rows with missing income because fewer rows and less signal always train better models
Impute the missing values and add a binary flag marking originally missing rows
Fill missing income entries with the corresponding loan approval outcome label
Replace missing entries with future values collected after the loan decision
q: Missing income values may themselves signal credit risk. How should you handle this column?

explain: Standardization centers features to zero mean and unit variance, helping gradient-based models converge. Min-max scaling or log transforms serve different goals like bounded ranges or skew.
options: Apply min-max scaling to force every feature into an arbitrary fixed range
Take the logarithm of each feature even when values include zeros and negative amounts regularly
Standardize features to zero mean and unit variance for gradient-based training
Multiply all features by large constants to emphasize the widest columns
q: Features span wildly different scales and a neural network converges slowly. Which transformation helps most?

explain: Scalers must be fit on training data only, then applied to validation and test, or statistics from held-out data leak in. Fitting on the full dataset before splitting is a classic leakage error.
options: Fit the scaler on the combined train and test sets together to capture the full value range
Standardize each split with its own separately fitted scaler for consistency
Tune scaling parameters by checking test accuracy after every adjustment
Fit the scaler on training data only, then transform validation and test sets
q: When standardizing features, which fitting procedure prevents leakage into evaluation?

explain: Clarify computes pre-training bias metrics such as class imbalance and KL divergence to surface dataset bias before modeling. Model accuracy and feature importance measure performance, not dataset bias.
options: Run SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics like class imbalance on the data
Measure final test accuracy because high accuracy alone proves fairness
Check training loss curves closely since smooth convergence alone guarantees unbiased input data
Rank features by importance because top features are always the fairest ones
q: Before training a hiring model, the team must quantify representation bias in the dataset. Which tool and metric apply?

explain: A large positive difference in positive-outcome rates between groups signals potential bias worth investigating. Equal label counts alone or overall accuracy do not reveal group disparities.
options: Confirm the dataset is fair whenever overall accuracy exceeds ninety percent
Compare positive-outcome rates across groups with difference in proportions
Count total rows per group because equal sizes alone guarantee equal outcomes
Average the loss across epochs since a low loss proves unbiased predictions
q: Clarify reports very different approval rates for two demographic groups. Which metric captures this disparity?

explain: Post-training metrics compare predictions across groups to detect models that amplify data bias, guiding mitigation like rebalancing. Retraining on the same biased labels without checks preserves the problem.
options: Delete the protected attribute column and assume all resulting bias disappears
Deploy immediately into production because biased training data never affects real model outputs
Evaluate post-training bias metrics and mitigate with rebalancing or constraints
Retrain repeatedly on identical labels until the disparity metric looks better
q: Pre-training metrics show strong label bias against one group. What is the sound next step before deployment?

explain: Including data only available after the label, like post-diagnosis codes, leaks the answer and inflates offline accuracy. Genuinely historical features or proper temporal splits avoid this trap.
options: Add historical lab results recorded well before the prediction cutoff time
Split records by patient admission date to keep evaluation strictly forward
Use only features whose timestamps precede the label definition moment
Include post-diagnosis billing codes assigned after the outcome occurred
q: A readmission model scores 99% offline but fails live. The features include post-discharge billing codes. What went wrong?

explain: Temporal or grouped splits with a strict cutoff ensure no future information trains models evaluated on later data. Random shuffles mix future rows into training and hide leakage.
options: Split by time with a cutoff so training only sees data before validation rows
Shuffle all dated rows randomly so future records freely mix into the historical training set
Duplicate high-performing recent rows into both training and test partitions
Select test rows by highest label values to make evaluation sets look strong
q: For a demand-forecasting model over three years of sales, which split strategy best prevents temporal leakage?

explain: Separate train, validation, and test sets isolate fitting, tuning, and final estimation so tuning cannot overfit the reported metric. Tuning on the test set or skipping validation biases results.
options: Tune every hyperparameter directly on the test set to get the best possible reported score
Use train for fitting, validation for tuning, and a held-out test for reporting
Reuse the training set for final reporting since it contains the most rows
Skip validation entirely and pick hyperparameters by intuition before testing
q: Why does a proper ML workflow need distinct train, validation, and test splits?

explain: Stratified sampling preserves the rare-class rate in every split so validation reflects reality. Pure random splits of rare events can produce folds with zero positives.
options: Oversample the test set with positives until classes look artificially balanced
Split rows alphabetically by customer name to keep the process deterministic
Apply stratified sampling so each split keeps the original 2% fraud rate
Put all fraud cases in training and evaluate only on legitimate transactions
q: A fraud dataset has only 2% positives. How should splits preserve this rate for reliable evaluation?

explain: Group-aware splitting keeps all rows of one customer in a single partition, preventing near-duplicate leakage. Random row splits scatter a customer's history across train and test.
options: Shuffle individual transactions randomly across train and test partitions
Duplicate each customer record into every split to maximize data reuse
Sort rows by transaction amount and cut the sorted list into three parts
Group by customer so all rows of one customer stay in a single split
q: One customer contributes many correlated transactions. How should you split to avoid leaking customer patterns?

explain: Cross-validation averages performance over multiple folds, giving stabler estimates on small datasets than one noisy split. A single tiny test set or tuning on test data misleads badly.
options: Use stratified k-fold cross-validation to average metrics over several folds
Rely on a single fifty-row test set as the definitive performance estimate for deployment decisions
Tune hyperparameters on the test set until the reported score looks strong
Train on the full dataset and report the training error as the final result
q: With only 800 labeled rows, a single split gives unstable accuracy estimates. Which evaluation approach is stablest?

explain: Accuracy is misleading on skewed data, while precision, recall, F1, or AUC-PR reveal minority-class performance. Optimizing raw accuracy favors the majority class.
options: Report accuracy only because ninety-eight percent always means a good model
Track precision, recall, F1, or AUC-PR instead of relying on raw accuracy
Compare models by training speed since faster convergence implies fairness
Use mean squared error because it handles imbalanced classes automatically
q: A 98%-negative dataset yields 98% accuracy from a model predicting all negatives. Which metric exposes the failure?

explain: SMOTE and similar oversampling apply to training folds only; augmenting validation or test distorts the real distribution being measured. Resampling must stay inside the training side of each fold.
options: Oversample the test set with synthetic positives to make scores look higher
Duplicate validation rows with positives so tuning favors the minority class
Apply SMOTE to training folds only and keep validation folds representative
Generate synthetic rows before splitting so copies land in every partition
q: Where in the pipeline should SMOTE oversampling be applied for imbalanced data?

explain: Higher class weights penalize minority errors more, letting the model learn rare cases without changing the data distribution. Lowering weights or subsampling the test set hides the problem.
options: Reduce the minority class weight to zero so the optimizer ignores rare rows
Subsample the test set to remove positives and simplify the evaluation task
Train much longer on majority rows because extra epochs alone fix class imbalance by itself
Set higher class weights so minority-class errors cost more during training
q: Without resampling data, how can a classifier be pushed to detect a rare 1% positive class?

explain: Undersampling the majority plus stratified splits keeps evaluation honest while easing training imbalance; discarding all majority data or balancing the test set distorts measurement.
options: Discard all majority rows permanently and evaluate model quality only on minority samples alone
Combine random majority undersampling for training with stratified evaluation
Balance the test set artificially so reported metrics ignore the true skew
Duplicate minority rows into the test set until both classes appear equal
q: Training on 500K rows with 0.5% positives is slow and skewed. Which combined strategy handles scale and imbalance?
A team keeps raw ML datasets in Amazon S3 and needs automatic cost savings as data ages from hot training use to long-term retention. Which S3 capability should they configure?
options: S3 Transfer Acceleration on all data lake buckets
S3 Object Lock in legal hold mode on every training prefix
S3 Lifecycle rules that transition objects to Infrequent Access and Glacier tiers
S3 cross-origin resource sharing rules for browser uploads
explain: Lifecycle rules move aging objects to cheaper storage classes automatically, cutting data lake cost. Object Lock, Transfer Acceleration, and CORS solve immutability, upload speed, and browser access, not tiered retention.

q: An engineer must retrieve only a few columns from a large CSV object in S3 for a quick data check, without downloading the whole file. Which feature fits?
options: Replicate the bucket to a second Region and read from there
Enable S3 Versioning and restore a previous object version
Use S3 Select to run SQL filtering directly on the object
Attach an S3 event notification to every GET request
explain: S3 Select pushes SQL projection and filtering down to the object, returning only matching bytes. Replication and versioning do not reduce the bytes read for one lookup.

q: Training data in S3 changes frequently and a bad overwrite corrupted a curated prefix last week. How can the team recover earlier versions of the objects?
options: Turn on S3 Requester Pays for the curated prefix
Enable S3 access logging on the training bucket
Enable S3 Versioning so overwritten objects keep restorable prior versions
Configure S3 static website hosting for the bucket
explain: Versioning preserves prior object versions so accidental overwrites or deletes can be restored. Access logging tracks requests and Requester Pays shifts cost, neither recovers data.

q: A company migrates an on-premises NFS file share with 40 TB of labeled images to S3 for SageMaker training. Which service moves the data fastest with minimal setup?
options: Amazon Athena with CTAS queries over the NFS mount
AWS Database Migration Service with a replication instance
AWS DataSync with an on-premises agent replicating into S3
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with one shard per folder
explain: DataSync is built for bulk NFS/SMB to S3 transfers with scheduling and validation. DMS migrates databases, while Athena and Kinesis do not copy file shares.

q: A MySQL database holds customer history that must be loaded continuously into S3 for a churn model, including ongoing changes. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon EMR with a long-running Presto cluster
AWS Glue DataBrew with a manual recipe run
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler with a local CSV import
AWS Database Migration Service with change data capture to S3
explain: DMS replicates tables plus ongoing CDC changes into S3 in Parquet or CSV form for ML. EMR and visual prep tools do not capture database change streams natively.

q: IoT sensors emit 50,000 events per second that need SQL-style windowed aggregations before reaching the feature pipeline, with exactly-once state handling. Which AWS analytics option fits?
options: Amazon MSK with a self-managed MirrorMaker cluster
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink on a Kinesis data stream
Amazon S3 Batch Operations with Lambda per object
AWS Glue DataBrew scheduled on static CSV exports
explain: Managed Flink provides stateful streaming SQL and windowed aggregations over Kinesis streams. MSK needs self-managed processing code, and batch tools cannot do sub-second windows.

q: A team already runs Apache Kafka clients and needs a managed Kafka-compatible broker to stream click events into ML pipelines. Which service should they pick?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with a Lambda transform
Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK)
Amazon Athena federated query with a Kafka connector
AWS Glue DataBrew with a streaming dataset
explain: MSK offers managed Kafka brokers compatible with existing Kafka producers and consumers. Firehose is delivery-only and Athena/DataBrew are batch-oriented query and prep tools.

q: A Glue ETL job joins RDS orders with S3 click logs nightly and developers want a visual, low-code authoring experience with generated Spark code. Which option fits?
options: Amazon Athena workgroups with per-query limits
Amazon SageMaker Clarify with bias metric jobs
AWS Glue Studio with visual jobs that generate Spark code
Amazon S3 Access Points with alias ARNs
explain: Glue Studio gives a visual canvas for ETL jobs and emits Spark code for RDS plus S3 sources. Clarify measures bias, workgroups control query cost, and access points manage S3 permissions.

q: A Glue job fails silently when malformed dates appear in source files. The team wants automatic data-quality rules that stop bad batches before training. Which Glue feature should they add?
options: Glue custom classifiers that only infer file delimiters
Glue job bookmarks reset on every single run
AWS Glue Data Quality with rule sets evaluated on the dataset
Glue DevEndpoints kept running for interactive coding
explain: Glue Data Quality runs DQDL rules such as freshness and format checks and can fail or alert on violations. Bookmarks track processed files, classifiers parse formats, and DevEndpoints aid debugging.

q: A pipeline must transform 20 GB of daily logs with Spark but the team wants no cluster management and automatic scaling. Which compute option is most operationally efficient?
options: Amazon EMR on EC2 with manually resized core nodes
AWS Glue ETL with serverless Spark and automatic worker scaling
Self-managed Spark on a fixed fleet of EC2 instances
Amazon Athena with long-running interactive sessions
explain: Glue ETL runs serverless Spark with automatic scaling and pay-per-second billing for batch transforms. EMR on EC2 needs cluster sizing, and Athena is a query engine rather than an ETL runner.
source: Adattata da Udemy – practice test MLA-C01

q: A DataBrew project profiles a customer table and finds skewed age values plus duplicate emails. Which built-in capability helps document these issues for stakeholders?
options: DataBrew CloudTrail digest file validation report
DataBrew IAM policy simulator for role testing
DataBrew VPC endpoint policy for network checks
DataBrew data profile with statistics, distributions, and data lineage view
explain: DataBrew profiling generates column statistics, value distributions, and lineage that make quality issues visible. IAM, networking, and CloudTrail options address security rather than data content.

q: A DataBrew recipe must run after each partner CSV upload, then publish results partitioned by date for Athena. How should the team productionize the recipe?
options: Convert the recipe into Kinesis shard autoscaling rules
Copy each upload by hand into Athena workgroup folders
Email the recipe JSON to an analyst for manual replay
Trigger a DataBrew job on S3 events writing partitioned Parquet outputs
explain: Event-triggered DataBrew jobs apply the saved recipe to every arrival and write partitioned outputs Athena can query. Manual copies and email replays are slow and error-prone.

q: Two teams run Athena queries against one data lake and finance needs separate cost tracking plus per-team concurrency limits. Which Athena construct provides this?
options: Separate S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoints
Separate Glue crawlers with identical schedules
Separate KMS root keys shared across accounts
Separate Athena workgroups with limits, tagging, and query controls
explain: Workgroups isolate queries by team, enforce limits, and carry cost-allocation tags. Crawlers refresh metadata and KMS or acceleration settings do not partition query billing.

q: An Athena query joins S3 orders with a live MySQL catalog for a training extract. Which Athena feature enables SQL across both sources in one statement?
options: Athena provisioned capacity reservations
Athena federated query with a data source connector
Athena notebook checkpoints stored in S3
Athena query result reuse for identical SQL
explain: Federated query uses Lambda connectors to reach MySQL, Redis, and other sources alongside S3 in one SQL statement. Capacity and result-reuse settings tune performance rather than adding sources.

q: A data scientist runs Terabyte-scale Spark feature jobs only twice a month and wants to avoid managing clusters. Which EMR option fits best?
options: Amazon EMR security groups with open ingress
Amazon EMR on EC2 with always-on core nodes
Amazon EMR notebook storage with local disks
Amazon EMR Serverless with pay-per-vCPU job runs
explain: EMR Serverless launches Spark jobs on demand without cluster setup and bills per resource used, ideal for infrequent heavy jobs. Always-on clusters idle between runs and add cost.

q: An EMR Spark job reads S3 prefixes that other writers update while it runs. Which statement about S3 listing consistency is correct?
options: EMRFS consistent view must be enabled with DynamoDB metadata, because S3 listings are eventually consistent
Step concurrency must be set to the maximum so that listings catch up with the writers
Kerberos ticket renewal every few minutes keeps the listings aligned with the latest writes
S3 offers strong read-after-write and list consistency, so the job sees the latest writes without extra configuration
explain: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for new objects and overwrites, and strong consistency for list operations, so the EMRFS consistent view is no longer needed. Step concurrency and Kerberos settings do not affect listing consistency.
source: Adattata da Udemy – practice test MLA-C01

q: A team cleans data in SageMaker Data Wrangler and needs a custom pandas transformation plus a join with a second dataset before export. Which Data Wrangler capability covers this?
options: Built-in Glue Data Quality rule sets only
Custom transform step with pandas code and a join step
Athena CTAS statements run outside the flow
Kinesis hot-shard rebalancing inside the flow
explain: Data Wrangler supports custom pandas transforms and join steps inside the visual flow. Data Quality rules, external CTAS, and shard management live outside the flow canvas.

q: A Feature Store feature group holds click features with a 24-hour time-to-live for live lookup. What happens to expired records in the online store?
options: They are duplicated into the offline store with new timestamps
They are held in memory until the next training job
They expire and are removed from low-latency online reads
They are converted into Athena materialized views
explain: Online store TTL drops stale records from real-time lookups while history stays in the offline store. Expiry does not create views or pin records in memory.

q: Multiple teams must discover and reuse curated ML features with schema, owner, and description metadata. Which Feature Store concept enables this sharing?
options: Feature groups with a shared catalog of feature definitions
Kinesis enhanced fan-out consumers per team
Athena private endpoints per analyst laptop
Glue bookmark encryption keys per job run
explain: Feature groups register features with metadata in one catalog so teams can find and reuse them. Streaming consumers and private endpoints do not publish feature definitions.

q: A project needs 50,000 product images labeled with bounding boxes for an object-detection model, with human review of low-confidence labels. Which service should they use?
options: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth with a private workforce plus review
Amazon Textract with automatic table extraction only
Amazon Comprehend with syntax analysis jobs
AWS Glue FindMatches with ML Transforms
explain: Ground Truth orchestrates human labeling workflows with bounding-box tools and verification steps. Textract and Comprehend extract text or NLP signals, and FindMatches deduplicates records.

q: A dataset contains free-text support tickets with names, emails, and phone numbers. Before training, the team must locate PII to mask it. Which service detects these entities at scale?
options: Amazon Macie scanning S3 buckets for sensitive data patterns
Amazon Athena engine version upgrades
Amazon EMR ganglia metrics collection
AWS Glue Python shell job timeouts
explain: Macie uses ML to find PII and credentials in S3 at scale and reports findings for masking. Engine upgrades, Ganglia metrics, and shell timeouts do not detect sensitive entities.

q: A hospital builds a model on patient notes and must encrypt curated S3 prefixes with per-project keys plus audit every access. Which design meets the requirement?
options: SSE-KMS with customer managed keys and CloudTrail data-event logging
SSE-S3 with default keys and public bucket policies
Client-side gzip compression without any encryption
S3 Transfer Acceleration with signed browser URLs
explain: SSE-KMS with customer managed keys gives per-project control and CloudTrail logs access for audits. Default SSE-S3 keys, plain compression, and acceleration lack key scoping or audit trails.

q: A text classifier consumes support tickets of very different lengths. Which preprocessing step lets mini-batch training handle variable sequences efficiently?
options: Tokenize text and pad or truncate sequences to a fixed length
Sort tickets alphabetically before every training epoch
Convert each ticket into a small thumbnail image
Drop all tickets shorter than the median length
explain: Tokenization plus padding or truncation produces uniform tensors for batching without discarding most data. Alphabetical sorting, image conversion, and dropping short tickets waste signal.

q: An image model overfits because training photos come from one camera angle. Which augmentation approach improves generalization?
options: Random rotations, crops, flips, and brightness shifts at train time
Resizing every image to a single fixed thumbnail once
Removing all color channels from the dataset copy
Training only on the sharpest ten percent of images
explain: Random geometric and color augmentations expose the model to varied views and reduce angle dependence. Fixed resizing, channel removal, and aggressive filtering shrink diversity instead.
source: Adattata da Udemy – practice test MLA-C01

q: A demand model uses hourly sales and needs rolling averages plus lag features without leaking future values. How should the team build these time features?
options: Compute rolling windows strictly from past observations per timestamp
Average each row with the next seven days of sales
Shuffle timestamps randomly before computing rolling means
Copy future promotion flags into every historical row
explain: Causal windows use only data available at each timestamp, so no future information leaks. Forward-looking averages, shuffling, and copying future flags all leak the target period.

q: A team switched a Kinesis data stream between provisioned and on-demand capacity modes three times within 20 hours. Their next mode change fails. What is the cause?
options: Each stream can switch between provisioned and on-demand capacity modes at most twice within any 24-hour window
Mode changes have no fixed limit, so the failure most likely comes from a throttled IAM role on the producer account
Mode changes are limited to one per AWS account and Region per calendar day, shared by all of the account's streams
After the first switch to on-demand capacity, the stream stays in that mode until it is deleted and created again
explain: Kinesis Data Streams allows each stream to switch between on-demand and provisioned modes twice within 24 hours. The other options describe limits that the quota table does not contain.
source: AWS docs: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — Quotas and limits

q: Five analytics consumers each read the same Kinesis shard with GetRecords. They now get ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, although producers stay far below the shard write limit. Which change gives each consumer its own read throughput without adding shards?
options: Increase the GetRecords batch size to 10,000 records per call, so that each consumer receives more data per request
Register enhanced fan-out consumers that read through SubscribeToShard, each with its own shard throughput
Add a separate Firehose delivery stream in parallel for each consumer, so that each reads its own copy of the data
Raise the producer PutRecords batch size to 500 records per request, so that the shard absorbs more records in total
explain: The shared read limit of 2 MB per second per shard is the bottleneck, and enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own dedicated throughput through SubscribeToShard. Larger GetRecords batches and producer changes do not raise the read limit.
source: AWS docs: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — Quotas and limits

q: A team moves 2 million image thumbnails of 60 KB each into S3 Intelligent-Tiering because their access pattern is unknown. What should the team expect?
options: Objects move to Archive Instant Access after 30 days without access, which lowers the storage bill quickly for the team
Objects move to Infrequent Access after 30 days, at a higher storage price than S3 Standard, after monitoring fees apply
Objects stay in the Frequent Access tier, since objects under 128 KB are never monitored or moved between tiers
Objects are compressed and archived automatically once they reach 90 days of inactivity, without any retrieval charges
explain: Intelligent-Tiering does not monitor objects smaller than 128 KB, so they are never eligible for automatic tiering and remain in the Frequent Access tier. The lower tiers apply only to monitored objects.
source: AWS docs: Amazon S3 User Guide — How S3 Intelligent-Tiering works

q: A 40 TB training archive is read only twice a year, by batch jobs that can wait several hours for data. The team wants the lowest storage cost while keeping automatic tiering. Which Intelligent-Tiering configuration fits best?
options: Keep only the default tiers, because archive tiers cannot be combined
Enable only Archive Instant Access, because it is the cheapest option
Add a Lifecycle rule that expires the objects after 180 days
Activate the Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers
explain: The optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers store data that is accessed asynchronously, at the lowest cost. Archive Instant Access offers millisecond access at a higher price, and expiring the objects would delete the training data.
source: AWS docs: Amazon S3 User Guide — How S3 Intelligent-Tiering works

q: A nightly Glue Spark job uses job bookmarks and writes Parquet files to a curated prefix. After a bug fix, the team resets the bookmark so that all source files are processed again. What happens to the files already written to the target prefix?
options: Nothing is cleaned, because bookmarks track only source files, so the team must manage the old outputs itself
AWS Glue deletes the earlier target files as part of the reset, so the output prefix is rebuilt from scratch automatically
The reset restores the target prefix to its exact state before the previous run, including earlier partitions and their metadata
Each earlier target file is rewritten in place with the corrected records, so duplicate rows never appear in the output
explain: Job bookmarks track only source files, and AWS Glue does not clean target files when a bookmark is reset. The team must write to a new output location or remove the old files to avoid duplicates.
source: AWS docs: AWS Glue — Tracking processed data using job bookmarks

q: A computer vision team keeps its training images on Amazon EFS and wants SageMaker training to read them directly. Which requirement applies?
options: The training job copies the dataset from EFS to S3 during startup, so the data is staged before the first epoch begins
The images must already be in EFS before training, and the job must run in a VPC that can reach the file system
Pipe mode is the only input mode that can read EFS, so the team must convert the files to RecordIO before the job starts
The EFS file system can sit in a different Region from the training job, as long as a mount target is reachable over the network
explain: For EFS, SageMaker AI expects the data to reside in the file system before training starts, and the training job connects to a VPC to reach it. The dataset and training job must also be in the same Region.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Setting up training jobs to access datasets

q: A team mounts an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system for training jobs and wants to avoid cross-Availability Zone data transfer charges. Which networking setup meets this goal?
options: Use a subnet in any Availability Zone, because the mount is independent of the zone
Run the job outside any VPC and mount the file system through a public endpoint
Use a subnet that maps to the same Availability Zone as the file system
Create one file system per Availability Zone and mount them all
explain: FSx for Lustre uses a single Availability Zone to avoid data transfer costs, so the training VPC subnet must map to that same zone. The job also has to run inside a VPC, so a public endpoint is not an option.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Setting up training jobs to access datasets

q: A training job uses FastFile mode on an S3 prefix, and the team now wants to feed it an augmented manifest file. What is the correct conclusion?
options: FastFile supports augmented manifests as well, but only when the training job is also configured to run in File mode
FastFile reads plain manifests but not augmented manifests, so the team must convert them to CSV before the job starts
FastFile requires an EFS file system to resolve manifest entries, so the S3 prefix must be mirrored onto a file system
FastFile supports only S3 prefixes, not manifest or augmented manifest files, so manifest-based inputs need File mode
explain: FastFile is a file-system view of S3 that works only with S3 prefixes, and it does not support manifest or augmented manifest files. For manifest-based datasets, the team must use File mode instead.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Setting up training jobs to access datasets

q: A team stores clickstream data in S3 for Athena and wants fewer bytes scanned per query. Which two statements about columnar formats such as Parquet and ORC are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Each column is compressed with an algorithm chosen for its data type, which reduces the data read from S3
Predicate pushdown lets Athena skip blocks whose min and max statistics cannot match the filter
Columnar files must be stored uncompressed so that Athena can split them across readers
Athena can read Parquet only when each row is stored as a separate S3 object
ORC files are always larger than CSV files, so they are never chosen to reduce storage cost
explain: Columnar formats compress each column separately and use block statistics for predicate pushdown, so Athena reads less data. Splitting works with compressed files, and the other two statements are invented constraints.
source: AWS docs: Amazon Athena — Use columnar storage formats

q: A team wants a Kinesis stream to keep clickstream records for a full year, so that models can be retrained by replaying them. Which setting meets this, and what is the limit?
options: Set the retention period to 8,760 hours (365 days), which is the maximum the stream supports
Set the retention period to 30 days, which is the maximum for every stream in the account
Keep the 24-hour minimum retention and copy the records to a second stream for longer replay
Set the retention period to 12 hours, because the minimum is one hour and cost falls with it
explain: Kinesis Data Streams lets you increase the retention period up to 8,760 hours (365 days), and it cannot be decreased below 24 hours. The other options misstate the retention limits or add a copy step that the requirement does not need.
source: AWS docs: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — Quotas and limits

q: A Firehose stream transforms records with a Lambda function. On large batches the function runs about 7 minutes, and deliveries fail. What is the cause and the fix?
options: Firehose can run a transformation for up to 15 minutes, so the buffer size must be raised to 3 MB to allow the longer run
Firehose invokes Lambda synchronously with a 5-minute maximum, so the team must send smaller batches or speed up the function
Firehose does not support Lambda transforms on JSON records, so the data must be converted to Parquet before any transform
The transformation must be rewritten as an AWS Glue job, so that records are processed in parallel across many workers
explain: Firehose calls the transformation Lambda synchronously, and the supported invocation time is at most 5 minutes. Smaller buffers or a faster function fix the failure, while the other options misstate the limits.
source: AWS docs: Amazon Data Firehose — Transform source data

q: A data scientist built a Data Wrangler flow in SageMaker Studio. The nightly batch job runs on an on-premises scheduler that cannot call SageMaker Pipelines. Which export option produces code the job can run?
options: Export to Amazon SageMaker Feature Store through a Jupyter notebook, so the transformed features are stored for later reuse
SageMaker AI Inference Pipeline, which creates a serial inference pipeline that is deployed behind a real-time endpoint
Python Code, which exports the flow steps to a Python file that the team can integrate into its own batch workflow
Export data, which writes the transformed rows to a CSV file on the notebook disk for the scheduler to pick up
explain: The Python Code export writes the flow steps as a Python script that can run outside SageMaker, though the team may need to adjust it for its environment. The other options create a feature group, an endpoint, or a local file, not a standalone job.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Data Wrangler export

q: A Data Wrangler flow imports only the first 50,000 rows of a 10 million row file and applies Encode Categorical. In production, the category Peru appears only in the full file. What should the team do before exporting?
options: Remove the Encode Categorical step, because encodings can only be computed from the imported sample and not from the file
Use Export data, which re-samples the source file each time it runs, so that every run sees a fresh sample of the rows
Filter Peru out of the Athena query, so that categories absent from the imported sample are ignored in the production run
Refit the transformations to the entire dataset before exporting, so that the encoding learns every category in the file
explain: Data Wrangler computes transforms such as Encode Categorical from the imported sample by default, so categories outside the sample are missed. Refitting the transforms to the entire dataset fixes this before export.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Data Wrangler export

q: Which statement about scheduling a Data Wrangler job is correct?
options: Schedules use CRON or rate expressions, and EventBridge starts the job as a SageMaker pipeline step on that cadence
Schedules are triggered automatically whenever a new object lands in the source S3 bucket, with no extra setup needed
Schedules run inside the notebook kernel, so the notebook must stay open for the whole duration of each scheduled run
Schedules can be attached only to Feature Store destinations, while S3 destinations must be run by hand each time
explain: A Data Wrangler schedule is time-based, defined with CRON, rate, recurring, or specific-time settings, and EventBridge starts the processing job as a pipeline step. It does not react to file arrivals, and it is not tied to a notebook session.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Data Wrangler export

q: A training pipeline calls PutRecord on a Feature Store feature group that has an offline store. Two minutes later a training job reads the offline store in S3, and some new records are missing. What explains this?
options: The offline store writes synchronously, so the missing rows must have failed validation and been rejected by the service
Offline store writes are buffered and batched, and can take up to 15 minutes to reach S3, so the pipeline must wait or read the online store
The offline store keeps only the latest record per identifier, so earlier rows for the same identifier were overwritten
Training jobs cannot read the offline store until the feature group is deleted and created again with the same schema
explain: PutRecord data is buffered, batched, and written to the offline store in S3 within 15 minutes, so very recent records may be absent. The latest-record-only behavior belongs to the online store, not the offline store.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Feature Store offline store data format

q: A team reads its Feature Store offline store in the Apache Iceberg table format and runs an incremental daily job that should read only new data. Which tracking method does AWS recommend?
options: Track progress by the write_time column, filtering rows newer than the last run
Track progress by api_invocation_time, which is set by the calling job
Track progress by Iceberg snapshot instead of write_time
Rebuild the whole table every day and compare row counts
explain: For incremental reads of an Iceberg offline store, AWS documentation says to track progress by Iceberg snapshot rather than by write_time. The other options use fields that the documentation does not recommend for this purpose.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Feature Store offline store data format

q: A privacy request requires removing a record from a Feature Store feature group that has an offline store. The team calls DeleteRecord. What does the offline store show afterward?
options: The original rows are physically removed from the Parquet files at once, so no trace of the record remains in S3 storage
Nothing changes in the offline store, because deletions apply only to the online store and not to the historical files
Athena returns an error for every query on that feature group until the offline store is rebuilt from the source files
A new record with the same identifier is written with is_deleted set to true, so the deletion is recorded in the store
explain: DeleteRecord adds a new offline-store record with is_deleted set to true for the same identifier, so the deletion is recorded rather than erased in place. Deletions do affect the offline store, and queries still succeed.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Feature Store offline store data format

q: A model uses clothing sizes XS, S, M, L and XL, where the order carries meaning. Which encoding keeps that order in the feature values?
options: Ordinal encoding, which maps each size to an integer that follows the rank order of XS, S, M, L and XL
One-hot encoding, with one binary column per size, so that each size gets its own indicator in the feature matrix
Hashing each size into a sparse vector with 4,096 dimensions, so that the model handles new sizes without a lookup table
Tokenization with TF-IDF, where each size becomes a term in a bag-of-words vector that the classifier reads directly
explain: Ordinal encoding maps categories with a natural order to integers, so the model sees XS below S below M. One-hot encoding discards the order, and hashing and TF-IDF are not designed for ranked categories.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Data Wrangler transforms

q: A team prepares support tickets in Data Wrangler for a linear classifier. Which two configurations are part of a TF-IDF featurization? (Select TWO.)
options: One-hot encoding of each full ticket as a single category
Min-hash encoding of each ticket into a 3-gram embedding
A standard tokenizer that splits on white space and converts words to lowercase
A Count or Hashing vectorizer that turns the token list into a sparse numeric vector
Ordinal encoding that assigns integers by ticket length
explain: Data Wrangler's text embedding tokenizes the text, vectorizes the tokens with Count or Hashing, and converts the result to TF-IDF vectors. One-hot, min-hash, and ordinal encodings are separate transforms that do not produce TF-IDF vectors.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Data Wrangler transforms

q: A company that has never used Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth wants to start a labeling project next month. What does the current AWS documentation say about this service?
options: Ground Truth is fully open to new customers, with new features added every quarter for accounts that sign up
Ground Truth is no longer open to new customers, although existing customers can keep using it without new features
Ground Truth is open only to accounts that belong to the Amazon Mechanical Turk workforce and its requester rules
Ground Truth has been replaced by Amazon Q for all labeling tasks, so the team should start its project in Amazon Q
explain: The current documentation says Ground Truth is no longer open to new customers, while existing customers can keep using it and AWS no longer plans new features. The other options contradict this status.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Training data labeling with Ground Truth

q: Which three workforce options can Ground Truth use to label data? (Select THREE.)
options: The Amazon Mechanical Turk workforce
A private workforce made of the company's own employees or contractors
A vendor company from AWS Marketplace that specializes in data labeling
Amazon Comprehend, which assigns entity labels from a trained model
Amazon Textract, which reads forms and tables for human review
The Amazon Q assistant, which chats with the labeling team
explain: Ground Truth labels data with Mechanical Turk, a private workforce, or an AWS Marketplace vendor. Comprehend, Textract, and Amazon Q are AWS services, not labeling workforces.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Training data labeling with Ground Truth

q: A team plans to shrink an EMR cluster overnight to cut cost. Which change puts HDFS data at risk?
options: Removing task nodes that run Spark executors but store no HDFS data, so the cluster keeps its full HDFS capacity
Adding task nodes on Spot Instances during the day, so that more executors can run during the peak data processing window
Removing core nodes that run the DataNode daemon while HDFS still holds data, which risks losing blocks stored on them
Reducing the number of YARN containers on the primary node, so that fewer applications can be scheduled at the same time
explain: Core nodes run the DataNode daemon and store HDFS data, so removing them while HDFS holds data risks data loss. Task nodes store no HDFS data and can be added or removed freely.
source: AWS docs: Amazon EMR — Understand node types in Amazon EMR

q: A team exports a Data Wrangler flow to an S3 destination node. Which two settings can it configure for the output? (Select TWO.)
options: A Kinesis stream that receives each output partition as a record
The file type, such as CSV or Parquet
A Glacier storage class that is applied to every output object
The compression method, such as bzip2, deflate, or gzip
An AWS Lambda function that encrypts each object before it is written
explain: The S3 destination node lets you choose the output file type, with CSV or Parquet, and a compression method such as bzip2, deflate, or gzip. The other options are not settings of the destination node.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Data Wrangler export

q: A team updates an existing Feature Store feature group from a Data Wrangler flow. Which two statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The dataset schema must match the feature group schema
Data Wrangler appends new columns automatically and keeps the old records
The feature group can be updated only if it has no offline store
All records in the feature group are replaced with the observations in the dataset
Each export can use a different record identifier for the same feature group
explain: Updating an existing feature group requires a matching schema, and the observations in the dataset replace the existing records. The other statements invent behaviors that the export does not support.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Data Wrangler export

q: Which two statements about the Feature Store online and offline stores are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The online store keeps the full history for time-travel training queries
The offline store serves sub-second real-time lookups for inference requests
A feature group must enable both stores, so an online-only group is not possible
The online store serves low-latency lookups of the latest record for each identifier
The offline store keeps records as Parquet files in S3, in either the Glue or the Iceberg table format
explain: The online store is a low-latency cache of the latest record per identifier, and the offline store holds Parquet data in S3 for training and batch use. The online store does not keep history, and only one of the two stores is required.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Feature Store offline store data format

q: A Clarify pre-training report shows a Class Imbalance value of +0.8 for the favored facet. What does that mean?
options: Facet d has far more positive labels than facet a
The dataset is balanced between the two facets
The model performs 80 percent worse on facet a
Facet a has far more training samples than facet d
explain: Class Imbalance is normalized to the range minus one to plus one, and positive values mean the favored facet a has more training samples. The metric is computed before training and does not describe model accuracy.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: Clarify reports a Difference in Proportions of Labels of -0.2 for a loan dataset, with facet a as the favored group. What does the sign tell you?
options: Facet d has a higher share of positive outcomes than facet a, so the disfavored group receives positive labels more often
Facet a has a higher share of positive outcomes than facet d, so the favored group receives positive labels more often
Facet a has twenty percent more rows than facet d, which is why the proportion of positive labels appears lower for d
The labels are normalized, so a value of minus 0.2 means that no bias exists between the two facets of the loan dataset
explain: A negative DPL means the disfavored facet d has the higher proportion of positive outcomes. The metric compares label proportions, not row counts, and a non-zero value does signal imbalance.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: A hiring dataset has equal counts for two genders, but the positive hire label is 30 percent for one group and 60 percent for the other. Which pre-training metric reveals this disparity?
options: Class Imbalance, because the counts are equal, so the metric shows the hire rates of each group in the dataset
Difference in Proportions of Labels, because it compares the proportion of positive labels between the two facets
Kolmogorov-Smirnov, whose range runs from minus one to plus one, so that it reports the gap between the two groups
Total Variation Distance, because it is restricted to row counts and therefore cannot report the label rates directly
explain: Equal counts give Class Imbalance a value of zero, so it cannot show the disparity. DPL compares the proportion of positive labels between the two facets and exposes the 30 versus 60 percent gap.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: A team needs a pre-training metric for a multi-category outcome in which a value close to 1 means one outcome category sits almost entirely in one facet. Which metric fits?
options: Class Imbalance, which compares the sizes of the facets, so that it reports how many rows each facet contributes
Conditional Demographic Disparity, which measures rejections by subgroup, so that it reports the outcomes within each group
Kolmogorov-Smirnov, whose values near 1 mean that label categories are strongly concentrated in one facet
Lp-norm, which has no upper bound, so that it reports the size of the difference between the two outcome distributions
explain: Kolmogorov-Smirnov has a range from 0 to 1, and values near 1 indicate that one label category is concentrated in one facet. Lp-norm is unbounded, and the other metrics measure different aspects.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: A Clarify report gives a Conditional Demographic Disparity of +0.15 for an admissions dataset. Which reading is correct?
options: Facet d has a larger training sample than facet a, which is why the admissions outcomes lean against the disfavored group
Facet a is rejected more often than it is accepted, so the favored group carries most of the rejections in the outcomes
CDD values are normalized and cannot indicate direction, so the sign of the report carries no meaning for the team
Facet d is rejected more often than it is accepted, so the disparity leans against facet d in the outcome labels
explain: Positive CDD values mean that facet d is rejected more than it is accepted, so the disparity leans against it. CDD is a directional metric, and the sample-size statement is a different metric (Class Imbalance).
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: A team wants a pre-training bias service that computes metrics on a raw dataset before any model is trained. Which service fits?
options: SageMaker Clarify, which computes pre-training bias metrics on the raw dataset before any model has been trained
Amazon Macie, which finds personal data in S3 objects and reports it in findings for security reviews by the team
AWS Glue DataBrew, which profiles and cleans data in a no-code interface but does not compute any bias metrics
Amazon Comprehend, which detects sentiment, entities and key phrases in text for downstream analysis by the team
explain: SageMaker Clarify provides pre-training bias metrics that are model-agnostic, so they can be computed on the raw dataset. Macie, DataBrew, and Comprehend solve other problems.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: A team trains on 2 TB of RecordIO files stored in S3. It wants a small EBS volume on each instance, plus managed sharding and shuffling across instances. Which input mode fits best?
options: File mode, which downloads the whole dataset to the instance before training starts, so the volume must hold all of it
Pipe mode, which streams data from S3 with managed sharding and shuffling, so the training volume can stay small
EFS mounting, which requires the files to be copied to an EFS file system in advance by a separate process each time
Local mode on a notebook, which keeps the whole dataset in memory on the notebook instance for the duration of the run
explain: Pipe mode streams the data directly from S3 with managed sharding and shuffling, which lets the training volume stay small. File mode needs room for the whole dataset, and EFS and local mode do not match the S3 streaming requirement.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Setting up training jobs to access datasets

q: A healthcare company must keep audit records unchangeable for seven years, even for the account root user. Which Object Lock setting fits?
options: Governance mode, which lets users with the bypass permission alter the retention settings or delete the object version
A legal hold alone, because it expires automatically after seven years and then releases the object for deletion
Compliance mode with a retention period, which no user can overwrite or delete until the period expires, root included
Bucket versioning alone, because old object versions cannot be deleted once versioning is enabled on the bucket
explain: In compliance mode, no user, including the root user, can overwrite or delete a protected object version until its retention period expires. A legal hold has no expiration date, and versioning alone does not prevent deletion.
source: AWS docs: Amazon S3 User Guide — Locking objects with Object Lock

q: A data lake administrator sets classification=confidential on a database and does not tag its tables. An analyst is granted permissions on the tag value classification=confidential. Which tables can the analyst reach through tag-based permissions?
options: None, because each table needs its own LF-Tag before the inheritance from the database can apply to the table
Only the tables that were created before the tag was added to the database, since new tables need an explicit tag
Only the database object itself, because the grant applies to databases and never extends to the tables inside them
All tables in the database, because tables inherit LF-Tags from their database, so the analyst's grant reaches them
explain: Tables inherit LF-Tags from their database, and columns inherit from their table. The analyst's grant on the matching tag value therefore reaches the untagged tables as well.
source: AWS docs: AWS Lake Formation — Lake Formation tag-based access control

q: A team tags S3 buckets and Glue tables with IAM resource tags and expects those tags to control Lake Formation access. What is the problem?
options: IAM tags define IAM policies, while LF-Tags are the attributes Lake Formation uses to grant permissions, so they differ
IAM tags can grant Lake Formation column permissions as long as the IAM tag uses the same key as the LF-Tag
Lake Formation requires an IAM tag on every column of every table, which the service does not support for tagging
Tags cannot be attached to Glue tables at all, so the team must move the data into a new bucket before any access
explain: Lake Formation documentation states that IAM tags and LF-Tags are not interchangeable: LF-Tags grant Lake Formation permissions, and IAM tags are used in IAM policies. Tagging the resources with IAM tags does not change Lake Formation access.
source: AWS docs: AWS Lake Formation — Lake Formation tag-based access control

q: A nightly AWS Glue Data Quality evaluation passes 45 of 50 rules. What is the data quality score?
options: 90 percent
50 percent
5, because five rules failed
explain: The data quality score is the percentage of rules that pass when a ruleset is evaluated, so 45 of 50 gives 90 percent. The other values confuse the count of passing rules with the score.
source: AWS docs: AWS Glue — AWS Glue Data Quality

q: A team wants to quarantine the exact rows that fail AWS Glue Data Quality checks, not just read a score. Where should the check run?
options: In a Data Catalog evaluation on the table, because that evaluation identifies the failing records for quarantine
In a CloudWatch alarm on the data quality score, which lists the failing rows in the alarm notification for the team
In an AWS Glue ETL job, because identifying failing records is supported there but not for Data Catalog evaluations
In an Athena view that runs the rules as SQL, because Glue cannot identify individual rows through any of its features
explain: Identifying the records that failed the checks is supported for AWS Glue ETL jobs, while Data Catalog evaluations report rule results without per-record identification. A CloudWatch alarm works on the score, not on rows.
source: AWS docs: AWS Glue — AWS Glue Data Quality

q: Which two Clarify pre-training metrics have a normalized range from minus one to plus one? (Select TWO.)
options: Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS)
Class Imbalance (CI)
Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JS)
Total Variation Distance (TVD)
explain: CI and DPL are normalized to minus one to plus one, where the sign shows which facet is favored. KS is bounded from 0 to 1, while JS and TVD range from 0 upward.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: Which two statements about Amazon Macie are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: It scans Amazon RDS tables directly for personal data, without any S3 bucket
It encrypts every S3 object in place when it finds personal data
It uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover sensitive data in S3 objects
It publishes sensitive data findings as events to Amazon EventBridge
It supports only custom data identifiers and no managed identifiers
explain: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 through managed and custom data identifiers that combine machine learning and pattern matching, and it publishes findings to EventBridge. It does not scan RDS tables, encrypt objects, or limit itself to custom identifiers.
source: AWS docs: Amazon Macie — What is Amazon Macie?

q: Which two statements about Lake Formation tag-based access control are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Tables inherit LF-Tags from their database, and columns inherit from their table
LF-Tags are the same as IAM resource tags, so they can be used inside IAM policies
Each table must be granted to each principal by name, because tags cannot drive grants
LF-TBAC replaces the Data Catalog, so existing tables must be recreated
A principal can access a resource when it holds a grant on a tag value that matches the resource tag
explain: Inheritance and tag-value grants are the core of LF-TBAC, and the access check matches the principal's granted tag value with the resource tag. LF-Tags and IAM tags are explicitly not interchangeable, and tags do not require recreating tables.
source: AWS docs: AWS Lake Formation — Lake Formation tag-based access control

q: Which two Amazon S3 features help meet write-once-read-many (WORM) requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
S3 Object Lock legal hold
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Transfer Acceleration
A Lifecycle rule that expires objects after a set number of days
explain: Object Lock uses a WORM model, with retention periods in compliance or governance mode and legal holds that stay in place until removed. Tiering, acceleration, and expiration rules do not prevent overwrites or deletions.
source: AWS docs: Amazon S3 User Guide — Locking objects with Object Lock

q: Which two statements about AWS Glue Data Quality are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Rulesets are written in Python and must be compiled before evaluation
The service works only with Amazon Redshift tables
The data quality score is the percentage of rules that pass when a ruleset is evaluated
A ruleset can contain up to 2,000 rules and is limited to 65 KB in size
Data Catalog evaluations identify every failing record in the table
explain: The score is the share of passing rules, and the documented limits are 2,000 rules and 65 KB per ruleset. Rules are written in DQDL rather than Python, the service supports more sources than Redshift, and per-record identification belongs to ETL jobs.
source: AWS docs: AWS Glue — AWS Glue Data Quality

q: Which three metrics are pre-training data bias metrics in SageMaker Clarify? (Select THREE.)
options: ROC AUC, a classification metric that summarizes how well a trained model ranks positive examples across thresholds
F1 score, a classification metric that combines precision and recall for the predictions of a trained model
Silhouette score, a clustering metric that measures how well each point fits its own cluster compared with others
Class Imbalance (CI), which compares how many training samples each facet contributes to the dataset before training
Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL), which compares the positive label rates of the two facets in the dataset
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL), which measures how far the outcome distributions of the two facets diverge from each other
explain: CI, DPL, and KL are pre-training bias metrics that Clarify computes on the dataset. ROC AUC, F1, and silhouette score are model or clustering metrics and are not Clarify bias metrics.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics

q: Which two SageMaker training input modes stream data without downloading the full dataset first? (Select TWO.)
options: File mode
Pipe mode
EFS mount with the data copied in advance
FastFile mode
Local mode on a notebook
explain: Pipe mode and FastFile mode both stream data on demand, so training can start before the full dataset is downloaded. File mode downloads everything first, and the EFS and local options do not stream from S3.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker AI — Setting up training jobs to access datasets

q: Which two statements about SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: They are computed on the raw dataset, before any model is trained
They require a deployed endpoint that returns predictions
CDD ranges from zero to infinity, and larger values mean less bias
A negative Class Imbalance value means facet d has more training samples
DPL compares only the rejection rates of the two facets
explain: Pre-training metrics do not depend on model outputs, so they run on the raw dataset, and negative CI values indicate that facet d has more samples. CDD has a range of minus one to plus one, and DPL compares positive label proportions, not rejections.
source: AWS docs: SageMaker Clarify — Pre-training bias metrics
